title: Best Carry-On Suitcases UK
short: Carry-on suitcases compared by capacity, build quality and wheel performance, from budget softshells to premium hardshells.
intro: A carry-on's real test is years of gate-checks, cobbled streets and overhead bins, not how it looks in the shop. This guide compares suitcases tested by OutdoorGearLab, which has tested 53 carry-on bags and travelled the world with its current lineup by plane, bus and train.

products.name: Platinum Elite Carry-On
products.best_for: Frequent travellers who want the best all-round organisation and durability
products.summary: OutdoorGearLab's top pick for years running, with self-correcting magnetic wheels that keep the bag rolling straight, chrome-plated zippers, leather handles and a dense ballistic nylon shell. Testers found it still looked nearly new after years of heavy travel, though it's on the heavier and pricier side.
cons: Dimensions slightly exceed some airline standards

products.name: The Carry-On
products.best_for: Buyers who want a scratch-resistant hardshell with a simple, effective packing system
products.summary: OutdoorGearLab has travelled with this to Nepal, Tibet and Australia, finding the extra-dense polycarbonate shell resists cracks and its flat finish hides inevitable scratches. A simple clamshell packing system with a compression panel works well, though it doesn't expand and the grab handles feel a little tight.
cons: Grab handles feel small and tight

products.name: Freeform Spinner
products.best_for: Occasional travellers who want a reliable, no-frills hardshell
products.summary: OutdoorGearLab's favourite cost-effective hardshell, reliable enough for a handful of trips a year, lightweight and with generous interior space for a long weekend or a full week of light packing. The trolley handle felt a little thin and wobbly, and the softer polypropylene shell is less tough than pricier bags for years of heavy use.
pros: Large packing space for the price

products.name: Carry-on Max
products.best_for: Buyers who want hand luggage that packs like a checked bag
products.key_spec: 49.5L capacity, aluminium-capped corners, includes stowable tote
products.summary: A genuine 'beast of a bag' offering around two weeks' worth of packing space, with a strong polycarbonate shell, aluminium corners and a trolley handle with more than 20 height settings. OutdoorGearLab notes its size means it may need gate-checking on fuller flights, and it can exceed weight limits on stricter international carriers.
cons: May be too large for some overhead bins
Can exceed international weight limits when full

products.name: Sion Carry-On
products.best_for: Infrequent travellers who want strong capacity at a low price
products.key_spec: 40.5L capacity, scuff-resistant polyester, removable toiletry bag
products.summary: A well-priced, sportier-looking softshell with a respectable 40-litre capacity and a laundry list of organisational pockets that OutdoorGearLab's tester genuinely liked. Quality inevitably suffers at this price, with small, basic wheels that struggle to keep up at full walking speed and a just-okay telescoping handle.
cons: Heavy and bulky at the front
Small, basic wheels struggle at speed

products.name: Baseline Essential Spinner
products.best_for: Buyers who want the most durable, best-organised bag money can buy
products.key_spec: 34.5L capacity, ballistic nylon, built-in suiter, non-zipper compression system
products.summary: OutdoorGearLab's favourite upgraded softshell, with a clever two-inch expansion/compression system, reinforced ballistic nylon exterior and robust, easy-glide zippers that stayed durable over years of testing. It's the heaviest bag on test and one of the most expensive, but the packing system and build quality justify it for buyers who travel often.
products.search: Briggs and Riley Baseline Essential Spinner

guide.a: A hardshell, like the Away or Samsonite here, better protects contents from crushing and resists scuffs with a wipeable finish, but can't flex to fit a little extra. A softshell, like the Briggs & Riley or SwissGear here, usually has more external pockets and can squeeze into tighter overhead bins, but offers less impact protection.

guide.q: What size counts as a carry-on?
guide.a: Most airlines allow cabin bags up to roughly 55 x 40 x 20cm, though exact limits vary by airline and cabin bins vary by aircraft. A bag right at the upper size limit, like the July Carry-on Max here, may occasionally need gate-checking on a full flight, even if it technically meets the size rule.

An expandable zip adds several extra litres of packing space for the return journey home, useful if you tend to buy things while travelling. It's a genuinely useful feature on an otherwise well-built bag, though it shouldn't be relied on to push a cabin bag over airline size limits.

guide.q: Is it worth paying more for better wheels?
guide.a: Yes, if you travel frequently. Premium bags like the Travelpro here use larger, often self-aligning spinner wheels that roll straight and glide smoothly, while budget bags tend to have smaller wheels that can feel wobbly or struggle to keep up at a brisk walking pace.
